TabCount technical report

TabCount: counting tablets from a phone photo with OpenCV 5 on AWS

OpenCV AI Competition 2026 (powered by AWS) · Technical report · Team TabCount

Live endpoint: {{LIVE_URL}} · Code: https://github.com/emediong-etuk/tabcount

1. Problem and real-world impact

Community pharmacies and patent medicine stores in Nigeria often dispense tablets loose, counted out of bulk containers of 100–1,000. Staff count them by hand, usually in fives with a spatula, at two moments: when dispensing a prescription and when taking stock. Hand counting is slow during busy hours, and errors cost money in both directions. Over-dispensing loses stock that is never billed; under-dispensing short-changes a patient. Stock-takes built on hand counts drift from reality, which hurts re-ordering.

Counting machines exist but are costly; almost every pharmacy assistant already carries a camera phone. TabCount uses that phone: spread the tablets in one layer, take a photo, get a count with an annotated image that can be checked at a glance.

2. Target users and usage scenario

  • Pharmacists and pharmacy assistants counting a prescription quantity (for example 30 tablets).
  • Patent medicine vendors who sell small quantities from bulk packs.
  • Clinic and pharmacy inventory staff counting partly used containers at stock-take.

Scenario: the assistant tips roughly the right quantity onto a dark tray (or white paper for coloured tablets) and spreads it into a single layer. They open the TabCount page on their phone, tap Take photo, and within about a second see “31 · HIGH CONFIDENCE” over an image with every tablet outlined and numbered. If it says “2 spots may be touching or stacked tablets. Check the orange outlines.”, they spread those tablets and retake. No install or account is needed: it is a mobile web page.

3. System architecture

Figure 1. OpenCV 5 components (blue) run inside a Docker container on an EC2 Graviton instance. AWS components are orange. Source: docs/architecture.mmd (Mermaid) and scripts/architecture_svg.py.

  • Client: a single static HTML page with vanilla JavaScript and no external resources. It downscales the photo on a canvas (longest side ≤ 1600 px, JPEG quality 0.9) before upload. This cuts upload time on mobile data and converts iPhone HEIC to JPEG.
  • API: FastAPI on uvicorn (2 workers). POST /api/count validates type (magic bytes: JPEG/PNG/WebP, otherwise 415) and size (≤ 10 MB, otherwise 413), runs the pipeline, and returns JSON with the count, confidence, warnings, naive baseline count, per-stage timings and the annotated image (base64). GET /health reports the OpenCV version, CPU architecture and EC2 instance type (read once from IMDSv2).
  • Persistence: if TABCOUNT_S3_BUCKET is set, the input, the annotated image and result.json are written to S3 as a background task after the response is sent. A failed upload is logged and never affects the user.
  • Observability: one structured JSON log line per request (count, baseline, confidence, latency, per-stage timings, image size, architecture, OpenCV version). No image data or client IPs are logged, and uvicorn’s access log is disabled because it records IPs.

4. OpenCV 5 implementation

The whole pipeline is in app/counter.py. It uses only OpenCV core and imgproc (imdecode, resize, cvtColor, GaussianBlur, threshold, morphologyEx, findContours, drawContours, distanceTransform, connectedComponents, dilate, watershed, putText, imencode) plus NumPy. None of the modules removed from the OpenCV 5 main build (Haar cascades, HOG, cv2.ml, the Caffe loader) are needed. The module refuses to import unless cv2.__version__ starts with “5”, and every API response reports the version.

Figure 2. Pipeline stages on one image: input, Otsu mask, distance transform, per-blob seeds, watershed labels, annotated result.

Decode and resize. imdecode with IMREAD_COLOR, which also applies the EXIF orientation from phone photos. Images are resized with INTER_AREA so the longest side is at most 1200 px (never upscaled). All area parameters are defined at this scale, so behaviour does not depend on the phone’s resolution.

Blur and illumination flattening. A 5×5 Gaussian blur suppresses sensor noise and tablet texture. Before thresholding, a smooth lighting gradient is removed: a quadratic surface is fitted to an 80×60 thumbnail of the grayscale image with iterative outlier trimming (tablets are outliers, the background is the majority), subtracted, and the image re-centred on the background level. Without it, on images with few tablets and a mild gradient, Otsu split the background itself into two classes (MAE 32.6 → 0.03 on a 40-image synthetic smoke test after adding it; see docs/DECISIONS.md).

Otsu threshold and polarity detection. threshold(..., THRESH_BINARY + THRESH_OTSU) separates tablets from background without a hand-tuned threshold. Polarity is automatic: the border band (3% of the shorter side) should be background, so if more than half of it is foreground the mask is inverted (dark_on_light, e.g. coloured tablets on white paper; otherwise light_on_dark).

Morphology and hole filling. A 3×3 elliptical close (1 iteration) bridges thin score lines and imprints, and an open (2 iterations) removes dust. Highlights and embossing can still leave holes inside a tablet, so external contours are redrawn filled, which makes every blob solid.

Distance transform and per-blob seeds. Touching tablets form one blob. distanceTransform(DIST_L2) gives each pixel its distance to the background, so each tablet’s centre is a local peak and the neck between two touching tablets is a valley. The usual tutorial approach thresholds the distance map at a fraction of the global maximum, which breaks when blob sizes vary: one large capsule raises the global maximum and the small tablets lose their seeds. TabCount normalises per blob. Blobs are labelled with connectedComponents, each blob’s maximum distance is found in one vectorised pass (np.maximum.at), and a pixel is a seed if dist ≥ peak_ratio × max_of_its_own_blob (default peak_ratio 0.5). For two equal discs of radius r touching with up to 15% overlap, the neck’s half-width is below 0.5 r, so the seed regions stay separate. For a single elongated capsule, the ridge above 0.5 r is one connected line, so it gets one seed.

Watershed. Seeds are labelled as markers (background = 1), the uncertain ring (dilate(mask) − seeds) is set to 0, and cv2.watershed floods from the markers on the blurred colour image. Labels ≥ 2 are objects; object pixels are intersected with the mask so the watershed cannot grow objects into the background.

Object statistics. Area, centroid and bounding box for every label come from one pass over foreground pixels (np.bincount for areas and coordinate sums, np.minimum.at/np.maximum.at for boxes). Contours for drawing are extracted only inside each object’s bounding-box crop, never from full-image masks per object. This keeps a 12 MP photo well under one second.

Debris and cluster correction. Objects smaller than min_area_px (60 px) are dropped. With at least three objects, the median area is the typical tablet: objects below 0.25× the median are crumbs (counted in debris_removed), and objects above 1.8× the median are flagged as possible clusters. These are tablets the watershed could not split, typically stacked or heavily overlapping. A flagged object counts as round(area / median) tablets. This is a heuristic, so flagged objects are drawn in orange (red for ×3 or more) and lower the confidence.

Confidence. high: at least three objects, nothing flagged, no warnings. medium: flagged objects are at most 10% of objects. low: anything else, including fewer than three objects and any contrast warning (no_tablets_found, low_contrast_or_background_not_detected, or background_region_detected when one “object” covers more than 10% of the image).

Annotation. Green outlines (orange/red when flagged), numbers in reading order, and a banner above the photo with count, confidence, time, OpenCV version and CPU architecture. debug=true also returns the mask, distance map, seeds and labels (Figure 2).

Baseline. app/baseline.py shares preprocess() exactly and then counts external contours above min_area_px. The only difference is the watershed and area logic, so the comparison isolates their contribution. The API returns baseline_count with every result.

5. AWS deployment

  • Amazon EC2 t4g.small (AWS Graviton, arm64) running Amazon Linux 2023 (AMI from the SSM public parameter), in the default VPC, with an Elastic IP so the URL is stable through judging. We chose Graviton because a small arm64 instance is enough for a CPU-only pipeline and the published OpenCV 5 wheel ships for aarch64. The container builds natively on the instance, so the evaluated code is the same arm64 build that serves users.
  • Docker: python:3.12-slim base (official image via the AWS ECR Public mirror), pinned requirements, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, --restart unless-stopped, port 80 → 8000.
  • IMDSv2 required, hop limit 2. Hop limit 2 lets boto3 inside the container reach the instance-role credentials through the Docker bridge. With the default of 1 the request is dropped and S3 uploads fail silently.
  • IAM least privilege: role tabcount-ec2-role (instance profile) may only s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/requests/*, and create and write streams in the /tabcount/app log group. No credentials exist in code, config or the image.
  • Amazon S3: a private bucket with all public access blocked, default SSE-S3 encryption, and a lifecycle rule that deletes requests/ after 60 days (data minimisation, long enough to cover judging).
  • Amazon CloudWatch Logs: Docker’s awslogs driver ships stdout to /tabcount/app with 30-day retention. A Logs Insights query in the README computes request count and p50/p95 latency per hour.
  • Security group: TCP 80 from anywhere; SSH only from the administrator’s IP.
  • Tooling: deploy/provision.py (boto3, idempotent, confirms the plan first) and deploy/deploy.py (build on the instance, replace the container, health check, smoke test asserting aarch64 and OpenCV 5).

6. Evaluation

Datasets. Real: {{REAL_N}} phone photos taken under eval/PHOTO_PROTOCOL.md: dark and light backgrounds; conditions separated, touching, stacked and hard (glare, white on white, broken halves, mixed types); 5–60 tablets per photo; ground truth counted twice by hand. The downscaled photos and labels.csv are committed, so judges can reproduce every number. Synthetic: 200 generated images (tools/synthetic.py, seed 42) with circles and capsule-like ellipses, radial shading, score lines, noise, blur, lighting gradients and soft shadows. They are separated, touching (pairs and chains with up to 15% overlap) or mixed. Synthetic results are always reported separately and are not evidence of real-world accuracy.

Protocol. Each dataset is split deterministically: about a third tune, the rest test. peak_ratio is swept over {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7} on the tune split only. Headline metrics are on the test split with the default parameters, which are the deployed system. A tuned value that differs from the default is reported separately and is never silently applied. Methods: watershed (full pipeline), watershed_no_cluster (cluster correction off; ablation), and baseline (naive contours on identical preprocessing). Metrics: exact-match accuracy, accuracy within ±1, MAE, MAPE, signed bias, by condition and by background.

Headline (real photos, test split, n={{REAL_N_TEST}}). TabCount was exactly right on {{REAL_EXACT}} of photos and within ±1 on {{REAL_WITHIN1}} (MAE {{REAL_MAE}}, bias {{REAL_BIAS}}). The naive contour baseline was exactly right on {{REAL_BASE_EXACT}} (MAE {{REAL_BASE_MAE}}). Turning cluster correction off gives MAE {{REAL_NOCLUSTER_MAE}}. Photos marked high confidence were exactly right in {{REAL_HIGHCONF_EXACT}} of cases (n={{REAL_HIGHCONF_N}}).

Synthetic (test split, n=133; generated images). Watershed exact 98% (MAE 0.04) vs baseline exact 29% (MAE 12.21); without cluster correction, MAE 1.20. The tune-split sweep picked peak_ratio = 0.6 on synthetic data; on real photos it picked {{REAL_TUNED_PEAK}}. The code default stays 0.5 unless the real-photo tune split supports a change. The synthetic set is easy by construction: single tablet type, clean edges, no stacking.

Latency. Server-side pipeline time per image on the evaluation machine (x86_64): p50 78.0 ms, p95 99.7 ms (synthetic, 1200×900). A unit test asserts that a 12 MP JPEG is processed in under one second. On the live endpoint ({{LIVE_INSTANCE}}, {{LIVE_ARCH}}), the benchmark of {{BENCH_N}} requests at concurrency {{BENCH_CONC}} measured end-to-end p50 {{BENCH_P50}} ms and p95 {{BENCH_P95}} ms from the client (including upload), server-side pipeline p50 {{BENCH_SERVER_P50}} ms, and throughput {{BENCH_RPS}} requests/s with {{BENCH_ERRORS}} errors.

Deployed consistency check. run_eval.py --url sent every test image to the live AWS endpoint: {{CONSIST_MATCHES}} of {{CONSIST_N}} returned exactly the same count and baseline count as the local evaluation run (match rate {{CONSIST_RATE}}). This shows that the deployed arm64 service is the system that was evaluated.

Failure gallery. eval/results/real/failures/ holds the annotated worst test images and a captioned contact sheet (docs/figures/real_failures_contact_sheet.jpg).

Failure types and their causes:

  • Stacked tablets (expected). A tablet lying partly on another shows as one blob with an unusual shape. Cluster correction recovers some of these through area, but a tablet hidden under another adds no visible area, so stacking causes under-counting. The orange outline and lower confidence are the mitigation.
  • Glare and specular highlights. Flash or a lamp creates bright patches that join the foreground on dark backgrounds, or punch holes that break a tablet in two on light backgrounds. Hole filling fixes small holes; large highlights can split a tablet (over-count) or merge neighbours.
  • Low contrast (white on white). When tablet and background grey levels overlap, Otsu has no valley to find. The pipeline then reports low_contrast_or_background_not_detected or no_tablets_found and low confidence instead of a confident wrong number.
  • Broken tablets. Halves are about 50% of the median area: above the 25% debris cut, so each counts as one. Whether that is right depends on the pharmacy’s policy.
  • Mixed tablet types. With two sizes the median is meaningless, so large tablets are flagged and over-counted.

7. Limitations

  • Single layer only. Stacked tablets cannot be counted reliably from a single top-down view.
  • One tablet type per photo. The debris and cluster logic assume one typical size.
  • Contrasting, plain background required. Patterned cloth, wood grain and white-on-white break Otsu.
  • Glare and very uneven lighting. Flattening handles smooth gradients, not hard shadows or specular highlights.
  • Cluster correction is a heuristic. round(area / median) is only an estimate. It is flagged, never silent.
  • Broken tablets are counted as whole tablets or ignored as debris, depending on size.
  • No drug identification. TabCount counts objects; it does not know what they are.
  • Real evaluation set is small (about 30 photos from one phone and one person); results may not generalise to every phone, tray or lighting.

8. Responsible use

  • A counting aid, not a replacement for pharmacist verification. The confidence badge, orange cluster outlines and plain-language warnings exist to prompt a re-check. The footer says “Always verify counts before dispensing.”
  • No drug identification and no dosing advice. The system never names a drug or suggests a dose.
  • No personal data. No accounts, no names, no prescriptions; client IPs are not logged. Users should photograph only tablets on a tray, not labels or prescriptions.
  • Private storage with automatic deletion. S3 objects are private, encrypted at rest, and deleted after 60 days.
  • Over-trust risk. Correct counts on easy photos can lead users to stop checking hard ones. Mitigations: any warning forces low confidence, numbered outlines make checking fast, and we claim no accuracy beyond the measured results.

9. Future work

  • Guided capture: live camera overlay checking contrast, glare and single-layer spread before the shot.
  • On-device processing: run the same OpenCV pipeline in the browser (OpenCV.js) for offline use.
  • Stock-system integration: send counts to pharmacy inventory software with the annotated image as an audit record.
  • Multi-type counting: cluster objects by colour and shape to count two tablet types in one photo.

10. Reproducibility

python -m venv .venv && (activate) && pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest                                              # unit + API tests, no AWS needed
python scripts/make_synthetic.py --n 200 --seed 42 --out eval/data/synthetic
python scripts/run_eval.py --data eval/data/synthetic
python scripts/run_eval.py --data eval/data/real              # committed photos + labels.csv
python scripts/run_eval.py --data eval/data/real --url http://ELASTIC_IP
python scripts/benchmark.py --url http://ELASTIC_IP --images eval/data/real --n 100 --concurrency 4
python scripts/fill_report.py

Pinned versions: opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 (the only OpenCV package), numpy==2.5.4, fastapi==0.162.0, uvicorn==0.54.0, python-multipart==0.0.32, boto3==1.43.118, Python 3.12. The full freeze is in requirements.lock.txt. Deviations from the original plan are in docs/DECISIONS.md.
